newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Likely Aleman win puts Nicaragua at crossroads.
newsitem.headline: Likely Aleman win puts Nicaragua at crossroads.

text.p: The apparent victory of right-wing lawyer Arnoldo Aleman in Monday's presidential election leads Nicaragua to a crucial choice: reconciliation or confrontation with the defeated leftist Sandinistas.

With just over a third of the vote counted, official results put Aleman almost nine percentage points ahead of his rival, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega, and above the 45 percent hurdle he must clear to avoid a second round.

Aleman, a portly ex-mayor of Managua and a coffee planter, is a strong and at times autocratic leader who vowed during his campaign to crush the Sandinistas. In a country still overcoming a past of dictatorship and civil war, his victory reflects a polarisation that could easily plunge Nicaragua back into conflict.
Ortega did not initially accept defeat on Monday, adding to fears of post-election polarisation.

In the second poorest country in the Americas after Haiti, where more than half the population lacks a proper job, Aleman faces an urgent challenge to rebuild the shattered economy and to do that he needs the help of all Nicaraguans. That includes the Sandinistas, Nicaragua's Marxist rulers from 1979-1990 who remain the backbone of the labour movement, the army and the civil service.

As he claimed victory early on Monday, Aleman suggested he would invite Sandinista support for his new government. "From today, I invite everyone from the other political parties -- from the one in second place to the lowest placed -- to unite forces. Nicaragua needs all of us to leave the past behind."

But he failed to mention a serious potential flashpoint -- the issue of property rights. Aleman has said he will seek compensation for some properties confiscated by the Sandinistas at the end of their rule, particularly those seized by wealthy party bosses.
Although Aleman has said he will treat poor people's titles with tact, low-income Sandinista supporters say any threat to their property will be met with force.
Doubts over whether Aleman will actually reach out to the Sandinistas in a conciliatory gesture or rub their faces in defeat have cast a shadow of uncertainty over the near future.

"Investment will be reduced for a time following either a Sandinista victory or an Aleman victory because both are extremes and there are fears as to how they will react after the election," Manuel Ignacio Lacayo, president of Coca Cola Nicaragua S.A., said before the elections.

Aleman plans to create 100,000 jobs in the 4.14 million population in his first year in office. To do that, analysts say, he will have to foster a surge in business confidence that will not come easily.

During a bitterly fought campaign that rattled many Nicaraguans in the political centre, Aleman battled Ortega with a rancour rooted in his arrest and the confiscation of his property under Sandinista rule.

Ortega, in turn, cast Aleman as a throwback to the rule of late ex-dictator Anastasio Somoza, whose family ruled Nicaragua through much of the century until it was toppled in 1979 by the Sandinista revolution.
Aleman does have Somoza sympathisers among his backers, chiefly those living in exile in Miami, and he has refused to denounce Somoza.
